summary: Best current practices for third party call control in SIP, where one party sets up a call in which the communication is actually between other parties. SIP allows several approaches, each with trade-offs, and this document discusses which are good to use. It is a best current practice, not a protocol specification.

eli5.summary: Imagine a receptionist who dials two people and connects them to each other, without joining the call. This explains good ways to do that using internet phone calls.

subtitle: Good ways for one SIP program to connect two other parties into a call, and which call flows to avoid.

tldr.problem: A SIP user agent sometimes needs to set up a call in which the audio or video flows between two other parties. SIP allows several ways to do this, and each has different benefits and drawbacks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes four call flows in which a controller sends INVITEs to both parties and relays their session descriptions between them. It recommends Flow IV for calls to people or unknown parties, and Flow I when the far end is an automaton that answers immediately.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice rather than a protocol. It also covers error handling, early media, preconditions and security, and says Flow II SHOULD NOT be used.

today: RFC 3725 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 85) published in April 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes practice for baseline SIP and does not define a new protocol.

sections.title: What Third Party Call Control Is
sections.content:
Third party call control (3pcc) lets one entity, the controller, set up and manage a communications relationship between two or more other parties. In the traditional telephone world it is often used for operator services, where an operator creates a call that connects two participants, and for conferencing.

SIP adds new uses such as click-to-dial: a user clicks on a web page to speak to a customer service representative, and the web server creates a call between the two. The call can be between two phones, a phone and an IP host, or two IP hosts.

3pcc works with only the mechanisms in RFC 3261, and many call flows will work with compliant user agents. The RFC exists because those flows differ in their benefits and drawbacks, and because extensions such as preconditions (RFC 3312) and early media make the picture more complex. In the RFC's terms, the controller is a SIP user agent that wants to create a session between two other user agents.
sections.eli5: A controller is like a switchboard operator. It calls two people and then steps aside so they can talk to each other directly.

sections.title: Four Ways to Set Up the Call
sections.content:
The basic operation is to establish a session between participants A and B, orchestrated by the controller. The RFC walks through four flows. All of them rely on the SIP offer/answer model: whoever generates the offer and whoever generates the answer end up with the media session, so if A makes the offer and B the answer, media flows between A and B.

Flow I sends A an INVITE with no session description. A's 200 OK carries an offer, which the controller forwards to B in an INVITE. B's answer is then passed to A in the ACK. It is simple and needs no SDP manipulation, but B may not answer right away. Until the controller can send the ACK, A keeps retransmitting its 200 OK, for 64*T1 seconds, after which the call is considered failed.

Flow II starts with an INVITE to A containing a "black hole" offer with a connection address of 0.0.0.0, and then uses re-INVITEs to swap descriptions. All final responses are ACKed promptly, but the controller must know the media types in advance, many user agents answer a 0.0.0.0 offer with a 0.0.0.0 answer, and the flow can fall into an infinite loop of re-INVITEs.

Flow III sends A an INVITE without SDP, ACKs A's offer with a black hole answer, then invites B without SDP and re-INVITEs A with B's offer. The controller does not have to guess the media, but it must manipulate SDP: build the black hole SDP, reorder or trim media lines to match, and detect when the two sides have nothing in common.

Flow IV is a variation on Flow III. The first INVITE to A carries SDP with no media lines at all, and A's answer has none either. After that the message flow is identical to Flow III, but no media manipulation is needed. The only change is to the origin line, so that the version increments by one and the other parameters stay unchanged. The limits are that A is alerted before any media is established, and both A and B may answer before it is known whether they share compatible media. If not, the call can be ended with a BYE, but the users have already been alerted, which can annoy them and may cause billing events.
sections.eli5: There are four ways the operator can introduce two callers. Some are quick but break if the second person is slow to pick up. The best all-round one rings the first person with an empty offer, then passes messages along once the second person answers.

sections.title: Recommendations and What Phones Should Support
sections.content:
Flow I SHOULD be used by a controller only when it knows with certainty that B is an automaton that will answer immediately. The RFC names media servers, conferencing servers and messaging servers as examples. For calls to unknown entities, or to entities known to represent people, Flow IV is RECOMMENDED. Flow III MAY be used instead, but offers no additional benefit over Flow IV. Flow II SHOULD NOT be used, because of the potential for infinite ping-ponging of re-INVITEs.

The black hole address 0.0.0.0 is an IPv4 address, so those flows are specific to IPv4. For other network or address types, an address with an equivalent property SHOULD be used. In most cases A hears silence while the call to B completes, which can be remedied by connecting A to a music-on-hold source.

Most of the work lies in the controller, and a standard user agent should be controllable by these means. Still, implementors of user agent servers are RECOMMENDED to support a list of features, including offers and answers with a connection address of 0.0.0.0, re-INVITEs that change ports, addresses, media streams or codecs, initial INVITEs with no SDP or SDP with no media lines, the UPDATE method, reliable provisional responses, and integration of resource management and SIP.
sections.eli5: If the second person is a machine that always answers fast, use the quick way. For real people, use the safe way. One way is so likely to go around in circles that the RFC says not to use it.

sections.title: When Something Goes Wrong
sections.content:
In every flow, a call to A is established first and then the controller tries B. That attempt can fail: B might be busy (a 486 response), the two sides might have no media in common, or the request might time out. The controller is RECOMMENDED to send A a BYE, which SHOULD include a Reason header carrying the status code from the error response. A phone can use this to play a local busy signal when B returned 486.

Another case arises while the controller is contacting B. A may send a re-INVITE with an updated offer, but the controller cannot pass it on because an INVITE transaction with B is still pending. The controller rejects it, and a 491 response is RECOMMENDED, as in the glare condition described in RFC 3261. A is likely to retry, and if that happens before the exchange with B finishes, the controller responds with another 491.
sections.eli5: If the second person is busy, the operator tells the first person why so their phone can make a busy sound. If the first person asks for changes while the operator is still waiting on the second, the operator says 'try again in a moment'.

sections.title: After the Call Is Up
sections.content:
Once the calls are established, both participants believe they are in a single point-to-point call. They exchange media directly with each other, while the controller is involved in two dialogs and sees no media. Because it remains the central point for signaling, it keeps complete control of the call. If it receives a BYE from one participant, it can create a new BYE and hang up the other. If it receives a re-INVITE, it can forward it to the other side, possibly after changing the SDP.

The controller need not just proxy messages. As a Back-to-Back User Agent (B2BUA) it can use any signaling it likes on each dialog. For example, when A hangs up it can invite a third party C and connect B to C, using Flow IV again.

When the controller changes SDP itself, for example to place a call on hold, it must increment the SDP version number. The other participant does not know this happened, so the controller must adjust the version numbers in later messages to match what each recipient expects. This processing also applies when the controller was not the one that set up the call but acted as a B2BUA on a call between A and B.
sections.eli5: After the introduction, the operator is no longer in the conversation, but still listens for signs of a hang-up. If one person leaves, the operator can hang up on the other or connect them to someone new.

sections.title: Early Media and Preconditions
sections.content:
Early media means a session is established before the call is accepted, usually to carry tones or announcements. The RFC shows two cases, both based on Flow IV. If B sends early media, B uses a reliable provisional response (183) in place of a final one, and its answer is carried in a PRACK rather than an ACK. When B finally accepts, nothing changes in the session and the controller just ACKs the 200 OK.

If A produces early media, the call has not been answered, so the controller cannot use a re-INVITE. It uses a SIP UPDATE request to pass B's offer to A. The RFC notes that media is likely to be clipped here: if A is a PSTN gateway, early media from the PSTN arrives before there is anywhere to send it, and anything delivered before B answers is lost.

Preconditions (RFC 3312) tie signaling to resource reservation. The controller can use them to ensure neither party is alerted unless a common set of media and codecs exists. In that scenario the controller sends an INVITE with no SDP but a Require header for preconditions, and the RFC RECOMMENDS the UAS answer with an offer in a 1xx response listing supported preconditions as optional. If B rejects the offer, the controller CANCELs the request to A and nobody has been alerted.

When A is the one that wants preconditions, the controller needs no special knowledge. It follows Flow IV and passes SDP back and forth, using UPDATE and PRACK when offer/answer rules require them. Both sides ring only after their reservations succeed.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you hear a ringing tone or a recorded message before anyone picks up. The operator can pass those sounds along, and can also wait until both phone lines are ready before ringing anyone.

sections.title: Example Services
sections.content:
The RFC gives two applications of these flows.

Click-to-dial. A user clicks a link on an e-commerce site and an HTTP POST goes to the controller. The flow is otherwise identical to Flow IV: the controller calls the customer service representative first, then the user's phone. The POST normally contains neither phone number. The user's number comes from back-end databases, since the user has presumably logged in, and the representative's number comes from provisioning. The RFC contrasts this with PINT, which allows calls only between two PSTN endpoints and needs SIP extensions, but lets the controller step out once the call is up. The baseline SIP approach needs the controller to keep call state for the whole call.

Mid-call announcements. For a pre-paid calling card, the controller can set a timer, and when it fires, put the called party on a 0.0.0.0 connection address and connect the caller to a media server using Flow I, which is allowed because the media server is an automaton. The media server collects the card number and hangs up, then the controller reconnects the caller to the original called party using Flow III-style SDP changes.
sections.eli5: When you click 'call me' on a shop website, the system rings the shop worker first and then you. For a pre-paid phone card, it can pause your call, play a message asking for more money, and then put you back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Authorization is the first concern. A third party call is indistinguishable from a first party call, so the checks that decide whether a call is accepted, whether by a human, a script or a service, must keep working. The new party is the one initiating the call. Ideally the participants would know both other identities, but that is not possible with existing mechanisms, so the RFC suggests that INVITEs contain the identity of the third party, who is ultimately the user requesting communication. That requires the controller to authenticate itself as that third party.

When the controller and one participant share an administrative domain, as in click-to-dial, the INVITE can carry a From field naming the representative and be signed with S/MIME using the representative's key. When the controller does not hold the participant's credentials, no standard way exists to delegate them, so the display name in From is RECOMMENDED to read "[controller] on behalf of [user]", with the URI identifying the controller.

For encryption and integrity, the controller is a participant in each SIP dialog, so S/MIME protection of the signaling runs between each party and the controller. Media security based on keying material in SDP can still work end to end, and even the controller cannot eavesdrop if it behaves. However, nothing cryptographic stops it from interfering with the initial key exchange, so it could insert itself in the media path if it wanted to.
sections.eli5: The operator has to show it is allowed to make the call for someone, and it could cheat by listening in. Phones just have to trust that the operator is honest.
